question: At a community wedding in Rajasthan, 90 of 150 guests develop acute vomiting and non-bloody diarrhoea within 4–6 hours of the meal. No secondary cases occur among household contacts over the following week. This outbreak pattern is most consistent with:

answers.text: A common-source (point-source) outbreak from a contaminated food item at the feast

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. All hallmarks of a point-source outbreak are present: a single shared exposure (the wedding meal), short uniform incubation (4–6 hours, consistent with preformed enterotoxin from Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus emetic toxin), a sharp single-peak epidemic curve, and absence of secondary cases. The attack rate is 60% (90/150), typical of food-borne point-source events.

answers.text: A propagated person-to-person outbreak caused by norovirus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Propagated outbreaks produce successive waves of cases — each wave separated by one incubation period — with secondary transmission among household contacts. This outbreak shows a single explosive peak and no secondary cases, which rules out person-to-person propagation.

answers.text: An endemic rise in background food-borne illness in this community

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. An endemic elevation produces a gradual, sustained rise in case numbers without a clear temporal link to a single event. Here, 90 cases occurred explosively within hours of one shared meal — this is a classic epidemic, not an endemic fluctuation.

answers.text: A zoonotic spillover event from animals at the venue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Zoonotic outbreaks require direct animal contact or vector-mediated transmission and typically show a different temporal pattern. The tight clustering around a shared meal with a 4–6 hour incubation and no person-to-person spread clearly identifies a food-borne common-source event.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the epidemiological triad and outbreak classification. This event shows all features of a common-source (point-source) outbreak: shared exposure, short uniform incubation, single peak on the epidemic curve, and no person-to-person transmission.
A sharp single-peak epidemic curve with short uniform incubation, shared exposure, and no secondary cases is the classic signature of a point-source outbreak.
